repairs.value: Harris argues that Kahneman’s experienced-versus-remembered-self distinction expands well-being beyond momentary pleasure by incorporating retrospective judgments about happiness, fulfillment, and one’s future into whole-life appraisal.
repairs.rationale: This revision restores Harris’s complete claim, supporting contrast, and limited consequence while preserving the frozen assessment and score.

repairs.value: Strongest feature: Harris directly answers Haidt’s aggregation objection through the experienced-versus-remembered-self distinction, broadening well-being to include retrospective judgments about happiness, actualization, future prospects, and whole-life narrative. Principal limitation: This establishes conceptual reach, not empirical validity or completeness, while Haidt’s immediate response preserves a distinction between remembered happiness and independently evaluated purpose, meaning, or accomplishment. Live burden: Harris must show why those value-laden assessments constitute well-being rather than separate moral goods, and how they can be compared reliably, without requiring this diagnostic reply to prove naturalism or defeat every alternative. Locked score: The assigned 80 appropriately rewards a coherent, responsive, clearly articulated expansion of the target conception while withholding stronger credit because retrospective reports do not establish measurement reliability, exhaustive coverage, or comparative superiority as a sufficient moral standard.
repairs.rationale: This revision ties the score to the reply’s conceptual success and source-specific evidential limits without altering any judgment.
